---
title: "Quiz: path tracing"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $N$ is the number of samples (paths) per pixel.

---

**Q1.** Name three effects a path tracer shows that a Whitted ray tracer cannot, and say for each why Whitted misses it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Whitted follows the mirror and refraction directions and shadow rays to point lights.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Soft shadows (a point light is either visible or not; an area lamp is partly visible). Colour bleeding (light bounces off a coloured matte wall in all directions; Whitted never follows those directions). Caustics (light focused through glass onto a matte floor; Whitted's shadow ray from the floor is blocked by the glass). Also glossy reflections.
:::

---

**Q2.** A path-traced image at 16 samples per pixel has a noise standard deviation of 0.08. How many samples do you need for 0.04? For 0.008?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Noise $\propto 1/\sqrt N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Half the noise needs 4× the samples: 64. A tenth needs 100×: 1600.
:::

---

**Q3.** A 16-spp render has a PSNR of 22 dB against a converged reference. Predict the PSNR at 256 spp.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
MSE $\propto 1/N$; PSNR changes by $10\log_{10}$ of the MSE ratio.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
16× the samples divide the MSE by 16: $+10\log_{10}16 = +12$ dB, so about 34 dB (+3 dB per doubling, four doublings).
:::

---

**Q4.** Why is a Monte Carlo estimate called *unbiased*, and why does that not mean it is accurate?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Average over many repeats versus one estimate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Unbiased: averaged over many independent repeats, the estimate equals the true integral. One estimate still has a random error with standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt N$; with few samples (or a large $\sigma$) it can be far off.
:::

---

**Q5.** A matte floor is lit by a tiny bright lamp. Directions are sampled cosine-weighted. Why do isolated very bright pixels (fireflies) appear, and what removes them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How often does a random direction hit a tiny lamp, and how large is the sample when it does?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A random direction hits the tiny lamp very rarely; most pixels never hit it (too dark), and the few that do get one enormous sample $f/p$ (too bright). On average it is right, but the variance is huge. Sampling the lamp directly (a point on the lamp plus a shadow ray, at every matte hit) gives every sample a moderate value: the fireflies disappear.
:::

---

**Q6.** A renderer samples directions with a pdf that is zero in a cone where a lamp happens to be. What happens to the image as $N$ grows?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can a sample ever see that lamp?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It converges, smoothly, to the wrong image: the light from that lamp is never sampled, so it is missing from the average. This is bias, not noise, and more samples do not help. A pdf must be positive wherever the integrand is.
:::

---

**Q7.** A denoiser turns a 16-spp render into an image with a lower RMSE than the 64-spp render. Is the denoised image "better"? What may be lost?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Variance against bias; recall the deconvolution day.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It has less error overall, but it is biased: the denoiser has smoothed things that were real, typically soft shadow edges, caustics and fine texture, which have no edge in the normal/albedo guides. The 64-spp image is noisier but unbiased. Whether "better" depends on what you look at: for measuring a shadow edge, the unbiased image is safer.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that cosine-weighted sampling, $p(\boldsymbol\omega) = \cos\theta/\pi$, of a Lambertian surface (albedo $\rho$) under a constant sky $L$ gives the same value for every sample. What is that value?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The sample is $f_r L \cos\theta / p$ with $f_r = \rho/\pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\dfrac{(\rho/\pi)\,L\cos\theta}{\cos\theta/\pi} = \rho L$, independent of the direction: zero variance, every sample is exactly the answer $\rho L$ (the outgoing radiance of a matte surface under a uniform sky).
:::
